I'm in the planning process for setting up a small satellite call center (25 people max). The building that is being purchased for the expansion does not currently have a backup power source. I am looking into alternatives that would give us the most bang for our buck. While we use an LP powered generator at our main facility, I was looking at the possibility of solar, wind, or fuel cells because of the reduced noise and possible tax benefits.

The building is in the US mid-west, nestled in the Great Lakes region, so snow is a possible concern.
Is solar a viable backup power source?

If you can have a large enough solar farm built it can supply enough electricity to power your call center, but you won't see any ROI on that for maybe 20 years. It isn't really a viable setup for redundant power because it's weather dependent and Time of Day dependent. For an electricity fail-safe you need something you know for sure is going to meet your power demands when you need them. Now, if you wanted to put a solar panel on the roof and run that electricity to an electrolyzer so as to create your own Hydrogen for fuel cells or another storage apparatus, that might work well and be cost effective. If you bought the hydrogen from a supplier, the resulting electricity can get pricey. Quoting from here.

Costs: Example 1: The cost of operating a 1kW fuel cell for 7.26 hours when only one cylinder is purchased per month is $134. This is equivalent to $18.40 per hour to operate at one kilowatt.

Costs: Example 2: When the number of hydrogen cylinders used is increased, then the cost is reduced. Assuming that 5 cylinders of hydrogen are consumed in one month, this gives 7.26 x 5 = 36.33 hours of operation. The cost of the cylinders is (5 x $100) + (5 x $14) + $20 = $590. This is equivalent to $16.24 per hour to operate at one kilowatt.

Of course that's for a relatively small fuel cell. Things get even more costly when you get into fuel cell stacks and fuel cells that can put out <400Kwh. The upside is that, unlike a traditional UPS, nothing is consumed unless you use it. Large-scale UPS systems have a high cost of ownership. (Not even going to try guestimating there, it can vary wildly).

I found this doing a search, which does a comparison of different large-scale UPS implementations. You could also use those solar panels to charge these.

I'm not an energy expert, so I could be wrong about everything written here, but I've done some research into alternative backup power in the past. Almost all backup power systems I have experience with incorporated generators or UPS or both, though.

Wow. Thank you for such a detailed and informational response.

Can I ask: based on your research, did you choose to go with solar? If so, did you take advantage of any of the available tax rebates/incentives (assuming you are in the US)?

Ultimately the company I was doing this research for decided that solar would take too long to see any real ROI, even with the tax incentives.. They chose the traditional diesel backup generator because it's cheap.

But there's a problem with that, too. Diesel backup generators are only rated for 200 hours of operation a year. Consider the Midwest and the tornado risk. What if nature decides to take out the grid for a week? Almost an entire year of safe operation has been used.

In my opinion, a solar + UPS or Fuel Cell setup is the most sustainable option. The solar panels will supply you with the electricity to fill the batteries/produce hydrogen, bringing down the cost of operation. In the case of hydrogen fuel cells, every canister you can fill with hydrogen just gave you a $135 return on your solar investment. You will see ROI quite a bit faster that way, at least only considering hydrogen in the cost of ownership.

I had a Time Warner Cable tech at my house a month ago and I asked him why I got shitty speeds when I was promised 100 mbps. His answer was that while everyone is paying theoretically to get 100 mbps, not everyone physically can. One big reason is that theres only so much bandwidth to go around and sometimes they have to prioritize where it goes. Another is wired vs wifi since wifi always gets worst connection quality than a wired connection. He said rarely will you get 100 mbps all the time, only real times you can get it is when the network is under very little to no pressure at like 2 or 3 am.
